questions.qtext:
An architecture provides an atomic operation fetch-and-increment(x), which atomically returns the current value of x and then increments it by 1. The atomic operation is non-preemptible.

The shared variable inside is a single shared atomic counter that is initialized exactly once, before any process starts executing the entry protocol. No process reinitializes inside upon arrival.

Assume that the value of inside never overflows.

$$ \begin{array}{l} \texttt{// shared atomic counter, initialized once before execution} \\ \texttt{inside = 0;} \end{array} $$

$$ \boxed{ \begin{array}{l} \texttt{// local variable to every process} \\ \texttt{int a;} \\[10pt] \texttt{do \{} \\[6pt] \quad \texttt{a = fetch-and-increment(inside);} \\[6pt] \texttt{\} while (a != 0);} \\[10pt] \texttt{/* critical section */} \\[10pt] \texttt{inside = 0;} \end{array} } $$

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.text: At most one process can be in the critical section at any time.
More than one process may be in the critical section simultaneously.
The above solution to the critical section problem is deadlock-free.

questions.qtext:
A single packet is sent from A to C through B. Propagation delays are: \(A \to B = d_1\) and \(B \to C = d_2\). Assume \(d_1 \le d_2\), and transmission/queueing delays are negligible.

Flow control is being implemented in two ways:

 
 

Case 1: End-to-End Flow Control

Flow control operates only between A and C. The packet travels A → B → C, and C sends back an ACK that travels C → B → A. The entire cycle completes only when A receives the ACK from C.

Case 2: Link-by-Link Flow Control

Flow control operates hop-by-hop. When B receives the packet from A, B immediately sends an ACK to A while simultaneously forwarding the packet to C. When C receives the packet, it sends an ACK to B. The entire cycle completes only when A receives B’s ACK and B has received C’s ACK for the same packet.

What is the total time for one complete packet cycle in each case (i.e., time to successfully send one packet from A to C and receive all corresponding ACKs)?

A. End-to-End: \(2(d_1 + d_2)\),   Link-by-Link: \(d_1 + 2d_2\)

B. End-to-End: \(d_1 + d_2\),   Link-by-Link: \(d_1 + d_2\)

C. End-to-End: \(2(d_1 + d_2)\),   Link-by-Link: \(d_1 + d_2\)

D. End-to-End: \(2d_2\),   Link-by-Link: \(2d_1 + d_2\)

questions.qtext:
Suppose a processor uses a prioritized Round Robin scheduling policy. New processes are assigned an initial quantum of length \(q\). Whenever a process uses its entire quantum without blocking, its new quantum is set to twice its current quantum. If a process blocks before its quantum expires, its new quantum is reset to \(q\). For the purposes of this question, assume that every process requires a finite total amount of CPU time.

Consider the following two schedulers that differ only in how priorities are assigned:

  • Scheduler A gives higher priority to processes with larger quanta.
  • Scheduler B gives higher priority to processes with smaller quanta.

Which of the following statements about starvation in these schedulers is correct?

options.text: Scheduler A can cause starvation because large-quantum processes may dominate the CPU.
Scheduler B prevents starvation since smaller-quantum processes finish quickly and free the CPU.
Scheduler A prevents starvation, but Scheduler B can cause starvation since new processes with quantum \(q\) may repeatedly preempt a CPU-bound process whose quantum has doubled.
Both schedulers prevent starvation because every process eventually returns to quantum \(q\).

questions.qtext:
We use the \( P() \) and \( V() \) operations on semaphores to prevent race conditions in user-level programs. However, the implementation of \( P() \) and \( V() \) inside the operating system itself involves incrementing and decrementing the semaphore’s count. Since these updates are also shared operations, they could potentially lead to race conditions.

This leads to a natural concern: are we merely relocating the race condition problem to the operating system and reinventing the wheel? How does the operating system most efficiently ensure that the internal operations of \( P() \) and \( V() \) are executed atomically?

Which of the following best describes the correct mechanism?

options.text: By disabling interrupts in user mode so that \( P() \) and \( V() \) cannot be interrupted.
By protecting only the small internal critical section of \( P() \) and \( V() \) using hardware-supported atomic instructions.
Operating systems execute kernel routines in a controlled environment where concurrent races do not occur.

By protecting only the small internal critical section of \( P() \) and \( V() \) using a purely software-based synchronization mechanism implemented by the operating system, without relying on any special hardware support.

A computer scientist needs to evaluate the performance of his computer in order to calculate the response time of an algorithm. Considering that all the sectors of track $0$ are read starting from sector $0$, then all the sectors of track $1$ starting from sector $0$, and so on. The disk rotates once in $30 ~\text{ms}$, and a seek takes $20 ~\text{ms}$ between adjacent cylinders and $80 ~\text{ms}$ in the worst case. Switching between tracks within the same cylinder can be done instantaneously. Assume that initially the disk head is at an arbitrary cylinder, and ignore the rotational delay i.e. the time it takes for the beginning of the sector $0$ to reach under the disk head (After every seek or track switch, the disk is assumed to be positioned at sector 0).

In this way, how much time is required to read a disk with $2,400$ cylinders, each with six tracks of $32$ sectors, in seconds?

The graphs in this question have no loops (an edge between a vertex and itself) or multiple edges (more than one edge between the same pair of vertices). A graph $G$ is constructed as follows: First, its vertex set is assigned to be the set $\left\{v_{1}, v_{2}, \ldots, v_{10}\right\}$. Next, between each pair of distinct vertices $v_{i}, v_{j}$, an edge is added with probability $\frac{1}{2}$.
